Chromatography
3) Synthetic Biology
Lecture 13: Gene expression and gene regulation (Prof. Somenath Bakshi)
Lecture 14: Synthetic circuit design and characterization (Prof. Somenath 
Bakshi)
Lecture 15: Cell free synthetic biology and Synthetic Cells
Lecture 16: Spare lecture or revision

Lecture 1
Nucleic acids structure, thermodynamics 
and kinetics

Lecture outline
1) Chemistry and structure of DNA and RNA
2) Hybridisation thermodynamics
3) Hybridisation kinetics

Learning outcomes
1) Describe the chemical structure of DNA and RNA
2) Describe canonical and non-canonical base pairing 
and secondary structures
3) Describe and use the two-state model for DNA 
hybridization to compute thermodynamic equilibria, 
melting temperatures and kinetic processes
4) Describe and use the Nearest-Neighbour Model for 
hybridization thermodynamics

Lecture outline
1) Chemistry and structure of DNA and RNA
2) Hybridisation thermodynamics
3) Hybridisation kinetics

Structure of DNA
• Backbone consisting of a 5-carbon 
sugar (2-deoxyribose) and phosphate 
groups
• Sugar joined by phosphates between 
the 3’ and 5’ carbon atoms
• Oriented from 5’ to 3’ “ends” having 
a phosphate and hydroxyl group, 
respectively. DNA is directional
• Phosphate groups are negatively 
charged under philological pH and 
repel each other

Structure of DNA
• Four nucleobases (or bases) can be connected to the 
phosphate-sugar backbone: Guanine (G), Cytosine (C), 
Adenine (A) and Thymine (T)
• G ad A are purines, with two rings
• C and T are pyrimidines, with one ring
• A base connected to the sugar is a nucleoside
• A base connected to the sugar and one (or more) 
phosphates is a nucleotide (nt), e.g. Adenosine 
Thiophosphate (ATP), Guanosine Monophosphate (GMP) 
etc. 
• A single-stranded DNA molecule (or strand) is a 
polynucleotide 
• If short (<100 nt), it is an oligonucleotide

Canonical Base Pairing
• Bases bind selectively in pairs: A with T and 
C with G, through canonical (Watson-Crick) 
base pairing
• Binding occurs via hydrogen bonding 
hence it is thermally reversible (very 
important for biological functions and 
nanotechnology)
• A and T form 2 hydrogen bonds (weaker 
bond), C and G form 3 (stronger bond)
• Bound nucleotides are referred to as base-
pairs (bps)

DNA hybridisation
• Under suitable conditions, two 
complementary single-stranded DNA 
molecules can bind to form a double-
stranded DNA duplex
• Strands bind with anti-parallel 
directionality
• Binding of two complementary DNA 
strands is called hybridization
• Some cations are required to screen 
phosphate charges and stabilize 
hybridisation

Double helix
• Under physiological conditions, double 
stranded DNA forms a B-form double 
helix 
• The B DNA double helix is right-handed
• Base stacking interactions between 
nucleotides stabilise the double helix
• Double helix is asymmetric with a minor 
and major groove 
• Structural properties: 
• Helical rise ~0.34 nm/bp
• Width ~2 nm
• ~10.5 bps (~3.6 nm) per helical turn

Double helices
• Other forms of double-stranded DNA 
exist
• A-DNA, also a right-handed double 
helix forms rarely in DNA duplexes, 
but is relevant for DNA:RNA and RNA 
duplexes
• A-DNA is wider and more 
compressed
• Z-DNA is a left-handed double helix 
that can form in the presence of 
negative supercoiling

Hoogsteen base pairing
• A type of non-canonical (non 
Watson-Crick) base pairing
• Hydrogen bonds occur between the 
Watson-Crick (anti) face of a 
pyrimidine (e.g. T) an the syn face of 
a purine (e.g. A)
• C needs to be protonated to form 
Hoogsteen base pairing
• G can form similar hydrogen bonds 
with itself (syn vs anti face)

Non-canonical secondary structures
Triplex
• A thirds strand binds to a 
duplex (in the major 
groove) through 
Hoogsteen base pairing
• pH-dependent due to C 
protonation
G-quadruplex
• G-rich sequences form compact 
“knot-like” structures of stacked G-
tetrads held together by G-G 
Hoogsteen base pairing
• Coordinated by monovalent 
cations
i-motif
• Analogous to G-
quadruplex, but for C-rich 
strands
• pH dependent due to C 
protonation

Structure of RNA
Same as DNA, but
• Sugar is ribose, with a hydroxyl group 
on the 2’ position

Synthetic DNA and RNA oligonucleotides
Short oligos of arbitrary sequence, used for:
• PCR primers
• Piece-wise synthesis of longer genes
• Guide RNA for CRISPR
• Small interfering RNA for therapeutic 
applications
• Biophysics and nanotechnology research
• ~$10B market size in 2025
Credit: Eurofins

Lecture outline
1) Uses of synthetic DNA and RNA
2) Solid state synthesis of oligonucleotides
3) Assembly and enzymatic synthesis

Solid state synthesis: overview 
• Oligos are assembled one nucleotide at at 
time on a solid substrate (resin/beads)
• Enables complete automation
• Synthesis scale from ~n mol to  ~m mol (~μ 
mol is typical)
• Enables inclusion of non-natural nucleotides 
and chemical modifications
• Used for both RNA and DNA
• Performed in organic solvents (e.g. 
acetonitrile)
• Yield decreases with product length, so 
limited to oligos with < 200 nt
An oligo synthesiser 
Credit: CSbio

Solid state synthesis: phosphoramidite 
chemistry 
• Phosphoramidite monomers are 
nucleotides in which functional groups 
are protected to prevent unwanted 
reactions
• Protective groups can vary, but the 
DMT group protecting the 5’ OH is 
always used
• Phosphoramidites exist for all 
deoxyribonucleotides and 
ribonucleotides (both for RNA and 
DNA)
A cytosine phosphoramidite
Credit: Integrated DNA Technologies (IDT)

Solid state synthesis: cycle
• Star with one protected monomer 
coupled to a solid substrate (bead, 
resin) through a cleavable linker
• Deblocking: Deprotect the 5’ OH 
group by removing DMT
• Coupling: Introduce the next 
monomer, which reacts with the 
unprotected monomer on the 
substrate
• An (unstable) phosphite triester 
linkage bond is formed between the 
two monomers 
Credit: Integrated DNA Technologies (IDT)

Solid state synthesis: cycle
• The coupling efficiency is never 100% 
(commercial providers claim >99%)
• The free 5’ OH group on unreacted 
monomers is therefore capped to prevent 
unwanted reactions with the subsequent 
monomer, which would result in 
undesirable deletion defects
• Capping of uncoupled bases can be 
achieved with different chemistries
• These capped oligos will no longer be 
extended in subsequent steps and will 
therefore form truncated products, which 
can be removed through purification 
(much easier to remove than deletion 
defects)
Credit: Integrated DNA Technologies (IDT)

Solid state synthesis: cycle
• The unstable phosphite triester bond is 
oxidised to form a stable phosphate 
triester bond 
• Unreacted compounds are washed 
away
• The cycle is repeated to add the next 
monomer, for the desired number of 
steps
• After the final cycle, the resulting oligos 
are de-protected to remove all residue 
capping groups and detached from 
the substrate
• Note that synthesis happens always in 
the 3’ to 5’ direction
Credit: Integrated DNA Technologies (IDT)

Solid state synthesis: cycle
• The detached oligos are finally 
purified by desalting, to remove 
all unreacted compounds and 
organic salts present
• Desalting can be conducted, 
e.g., with size exclusion 
chromatography, precipitation 
or diafiltration
Credit: Integrated DNA Technologies (IDT)

Solid state synthesis: yield
• Because coupling efficiency is 
<100%, the fraction of truncated 
products increases with oligo length
• For ~60-80 nt, the yield of full-length 
products can drop to <50%
• Standard desalting does not remove 
truncated products
• Alternative purification is thus 
required to remove truncated 
products, namely 
• High Performance Liquid 
Chromatography (HPLC, more on this 
later in the course)
• Polyacrylamide Gel Electrophoresis 
(PAGE, you have already studied this)
Credit: Integrated DNA Technologies (IDT)

Solid state synthesis: chemical modifications
• Phosphoramidite synthesis enables 
incorporation of arbitrary chemical 
modifications, either at the 3’ end, 
the 5’ end or internally
• Possible modifications include
• Fluorescent molecules or quenchers
• Reactive linkers to connect the oligos to 
other materials/molecules (e.g. click 
chemistry linkers)
• Spacers
• Modified nucleotides (e.g. methylated, 
locked) 
A 3’ fluorescein modification
Credit: Integrated DNA Technologies (IDT)

Exercise
Integrated DNA Technologies claims a 
coupling efficiency of 99.4% in their oligo 
synthesis process, as opposed to 99.1% of 
“other suppliers”. 
1. Derive an expression for the yield of 
full-length products vs oligo length
2. Estimate the yield for a 20, 60 and 200 
nt oligos for IDT and “other suppliers”

Solution
• If 𝑃 is the coupling probability, the yield 
for an 𝑛-mer is simply 𝑌𝑛= 𝑃𝑛−1
• IDT claims 𝑃= 0.994, hence 
𝑌20 = 0.99419 = 0.892
𝑌60 = 0.99459 = 0.701
𝑌200 = 0.994199 = 0.302
• For “other suppliers”
𝑌20 = 0.99119 = 0.842
𝑌60 = 0.99159 = 0.587
𝑌200 = 0.991199 = 0.165

From oligos to synthetic genes?
• For many biotechnology and synthetic 
biology applications one can start off 
from existing (natural) genes, and then 
engineer them by introducing mutations 
etc (you have learned this in biotech 
fundamentals)
• However, many modern applications 
require constructing genes completely de 
novo
• How do we go from short synthetic oligos 
to full scale genes?
Credit: Eurofins

Polymerase cycling assembly
• The simplest method to connect short 
synthetic oligonucleotides into long 
double-stranded segments of several kb 
(kilo bases)
• Start off with DNA oligonucleotides (~50-
60 nt) that share complementary overlap 
regions (~20 nt)
• Mix all oligos in equimolar concentration 
such that they can (potentially) anneal to 
form the target, full-length chain
Original reference: Stemmer et al, Gene 164(1), 49-53, 1995. Please read!

Polymerase cycling assembly
• Like PCR primers, it is required that the 
overlap regions between oligos have 
similar melting temperature and that the 
oligos are unlikely to form strong 
secondary structure
• Run ~30 PCR cycles with the mixture of 
oligos without additional primers
• During this PCR extension phase 
hybridised oligos will be extended the 
polymerase
Original reference: Stemmer et al, Gene 164(1), 49-53, 1995. Please read!

Polymerase cycling assembly
• Constructs of different lengths will be 
formed, depending on which oligos 
happened to be hybridised
• After ~30 cycles, there is a good chance 
that some of the full-length products are 
produced
• Add primers that bind the ends of the full-
length products and run additional ~20 
PCR cycles to selectively amplify the full-
length product
Original reference: Stemmer et al, Gene 164(1), 49-53, 1995. Please read!

Polymerase cycling assembly
• Potentially purify (e.g. with gel 
electrophoresis) to remove shorter 
products
• Can produce gene fragments up to a 
few kb under optimal conditions
• Creating longer constructs (e.g. synthetic 
genomes) requires alternative methos
Original reference: Stemmer et al, Gene 164(1), 49-53, 1995. Please read!
Gibson assembly

Gibson assembly
Original reference: Gibson et al, Nature Methods 6, 343–345, 2009. Please read!
• Start with two double-stranded 
gene fragments that share 
overlapping regions (~50 bp) at 
one end (black in the diagram)
• Overlapping regions can be 
added with PCR primers
• T5 exonuclease chews back the 
5’ ends, creating complementary 
overhangs that allow the 
fragments to connect

Gibson assembly
Original reference: Gibson et al, Nature Methods 6, 343–345, 2009. Please read!
• Phusion polymerase extends back 
the 5’ ends to reconstruct the 
excess digested regions
• Taq ligase then repairs the nicks to 
produce the target construct
• Can be conducted in a one pot, 
isothermal reaction at 50 °C or in a 
two-step reaction in which first one 
adds the exonuclease and then the 
polymerase and ligase
• The two-step reaction is preferred 
for longer constructs

Synthetic genomes: M. mycoides
Original reference: Gibson et al, Science 329, 53-56, 2010. Please read!
• Can incorporate very long 
constructs (up to 100 kb) and 
create entire synthetic genomes
• In 2010 Gibson et al (same guy) 
form the Craig Venter Institute 
(JCVI) synthesised an entire 
synthetic genome using these 
techniques
• They started from sequencing (next 
lecture!) information on the 
genome of Mycoplasma mycoides 
(a very simple bacterium with a 
short genome)

Original reference: Gibson et al, Science 329, 53-56, 2010. Please read!
• They then proceeded to 
assemble a fully synthetic M. 
mycoides genomes hierarchically
• Started from DNA 
oligonucleotides produced with 
solid state synthesis and 
assembled larger and and larger 
fragments
• For the largest fragments, in vivo 
recombination in yeast was used
Synthetic genomes: M. mycoides

Original reference: Gibson et al, Science 329, 53-56, 2010. Please read!
• The synthetic DNA was inserted into 
a recipient cell M. capricolum to 
create a strain of M. mycoides with 
entirely synthetic genome, dubbed

• The JCVI team proceeded to 
produce subsequent iterations trying 
to minimise the genome and create 
a minimal bacterial cell. Current 
version is JCVI-syn3.0 (more on this 
later)

Frederick Sanger
• Cambridge-educated biochemist
• Worked at Medical Research Council 
Laboratory of Molecular Biology
• Wond TWO Nobel Prizes in Chemistry: one 
for discovering the sequence of insulin 
and one for developing the first method 
for DNA sequencing (shared with Walter 
Gilbert and Paul Berg)
• The Wellcome Trust Sanger Institute is 
named after him
Frederick Sanger 1918-2013

Sanger sequencing
• Requires
• A single-stranded DNA template (that we 
would like to sequence)
• A primer
• DNA polymerase
• Deoxynucleotide triphosphates (dNTPs)
• Dideoxinucleotide triphosphates (ddNTPs)
• (other co-factors for the polymerisation 
reaction)
Dideoxinucleotide 
triphosphate (ddATP)
Deoxinucleotide 
triphosphate (dATP)

Sanger sequencing
• ddNTPs lack the OH group on the 3’ 
carbon of the sugar
• When a ddNTP is incorporates in the 
nascent DNA chain by the polymerase, 
elongation will terminate as no bond can 
be made with subsequent nucleotides
Dideoxinucleotide 
triphosphate (ddATP)

Sanger sequencing
• In Sanger sequencing, a polymerisation 
reaction is run in the presence of a small 
amount of ddNTPs (~1%), alongside dNTPs
• Occasionally, a ddNTP will be 
incorporated in the DNA chain, which 
causes elongation to stop and produces 
a truncated product
• Electrophoresis can then be used to 
detect the truncated products
Credit: AAT Sigma-Aldrich

Sanger sequencing
• In early implementations, one had to run 
four parallel reactions, each of which 
included only one of the four possible 
ddNTPs: ddATP, ddTTP, ddCTP and ddGTP
• In each reaction truncation would 
therefore occur only at the locations in 
the sequence matching the 
corresponding nucleotide
• Running electrophoresis of the four 
reactions in parallel enables sequence 
reconstruction
Radioactively labelled 
sequencing gel

Sanger sequencing
• Introduction of fluorescently labelled 
ddNTPs enabled sequencing to be run as 
a single reaction
• The four ddNTPs are labelled with 
spectrally distinct fluorophores (emitting 
light at different wavelength)

Sanger sequencing
All truncated fragments will 
therefore be labelled with a 
different fluorophore 
depending on the final (3’) 
base
Credit: AAT bioquest

Sanger sequencing
• Capillary electrophoresis can 
then be used to separate 
truncated products by length 
AND identify the final 
nucleotide using fluorescence
• Sequence can be read from 
the output chromatogram, 
namely from the sequence of 
peaks (bands) observed at 
the different wavelengths
Credit: AAT bioquest

Sanger sequencing
Advantages
• The process can be automated with stand alone machines
• It is very accurate, up to 99.99%
• It can produce relatively long reads, >500 nt
Disadvantages
• Low throughput 
• Cannot sequence initial bases (due to primer)
• Accuracy drops for longer constructs as it gets more difficult 
to distinguish products of different lengths by 
electrophoresis
It is still used routinely when high accuracy is required and 
low throughput is not an issue. However, for applications that 
require high throughput, e.g. full genome sequencing, we 
now use next generation sequencing 
Credit: ThermoFisher

Human Genome Project
• Project carried out by multiple institutions 
internationally to map the entire Human Genome 
(3 billion nucleotides)
• Costed about $3 billion, so $1 per nucleotide
• In the UK, work done at the Sanger Institute
• Mainly funded by the US government
• Started in 1990 and completed in 2003

How to sequence genomes? 
Shotgun approach
• Genomes are randomly fragmented using 
mechanical shearing (sonication)
• To create a sequencing library, individual 
fragments are cloned into plasmids and 
transformed into E. coli so they are amplified
• Plasmids from individual colonies are 
sequenced, to obtain the sequence of 
individual fragments
• Bioinformatics tools are used to stich together 
the sequences and reconstruct the entire 
genome
• The Human Genome Project used similar 
techniques

Sequencing Moore’s Law
Cost of sequencing 
decreased exponentially 
(Moore’s Law) until ~2007, 
then started decreasing at a 
much faster rate, plateauing 
at around $1000 per genome 
(that’s ~$10-6 per nucleotide!)
What happened around 
2007?

Lecture outline
1) Sanger sequencing
2) Next generation (Illumina) sequencing

Next Generation Sequencing (NGS)
• AKA Massively Parallel Sequencing
• A collection of techniques to greatly enhance 
sequencing throughput
• Sanger sequencing can sample ~96 strands in one 
go (one well plate), NGS can produce millions to 
billions of reads in one run
• Different techniques were developed, but one 
emerged as the dominant approach: Illumina 
Sequencing
• Technology originated from from S. 
Balasubramanian and D. Klenerman in Cambridge 
(Chemistry), who funded a company called Solexa, 
later sold to Illumina for $600M
• Illumina has an annual revenue of 4.37 billion (2024)
Prof Sir David Klenerman (left) and Prof Sir Shankar 
Balasubramanian (right), Dept. of Chemistry

Illumina sequencing: Library Preparation
• Break the DNA to sequence in 100-200 
bp fragments with sonication
• Fragments will have random short 
overhangs and need to be polished to 
produce blunt ends. This is done using 
exonucleases (to chew 5’ overhangs) 
and polymerase (to repair 3’ 
overhangs)

Illumina sequencing: Library Preparation
• Use Taq polymerase to add a non-
templated Adenine at the 3’ end. This 
is required to append Y adapters
• Y adapters have a 5’ T overhang and 
can be ligated to the adenylated 
fragments
• Y adapters at both sides are identical. 
They have identical 3’ and 5’ 
overhangs

Illumina sequencing: Library Preparation
• We can use the overhangs of the Y 
constructs as binding sites for a forward 
and reverse primer in PCR
• The primers can then be used to amplify 
the constructs with PCR and append 
different sequences at the two ends of 
the fragments, labelled P5 and P7
• It is critical that all fragments have P5 
and P7
• A barcode sequence (BC ~6nt) is also 
included

Illumina sequencing: Amplification and 
cluster generation
• We have now prepared the library such 
that each individual fragment terminates 
with specific P5 and P7 sequences at 
either end
• We would like to sequence as many as 
possible of these fragments in parallel
• To achieve this, Solexa developed a 
process called Bridge or Surface PCR, that 
produces millions or billions of clusters of 
identical fragments on a surface
• Each cluster (and thus each fragment) 
can then be sequenced through a 
Sequencing By Synthesis (SBS) approach
P5
P7

Illumina sequencing: Bridge PCR for cluster 
generation
• Consider a silicon-derived surface with 
a high density of oligos tethered, with 
sequences P5’ and P7’, 
complementary to the P5 and P7 
regions on the fragments
• The surface (microarray) is in a flow 
cell, and can be exposed to a 
sequence of reagents
• First, we expose the surface to 
(denatured) fragments, such that they 
will randomly attach to the P5’ and P7’ 
oligos

Illumina sequencing: Bridge PCR for cluster 
generation
• We then use a polymerase on these anchored fragments, using 
the P5’ and P7’ strands as primers
• We then de-nature the newly formed duplexes to release the initial 
fragments, obtaining a surface with a (relatively sparse) coverage 
of covalently tethered fragments
polymerisation
denaturing

Illumina sequencing: Bridge PCR for cluster 
generation
• The tethered strands can then re-bind to free P7’ pr P5’ strands on 
the nearby surface, forming loops (or bridges)
• We can then polymerise and de-nature once more, which will 
produce a new copy of the construct 
looping
polymerise
denature

Illumina sequencing: Bridge PCR for cluster 
generation
• The process is repeated multiple times (25-35 times) to generate up to 
thousands copies in the vicinity of the original fragment, forming a 
cluster with up to thousands of copies
• In some protocols, all fragments with one orientation are 
(enzymatically) cleaved, leaving the cluster with fragments all with the 
same orientation

Illumina sequencing: Bridge PCR for cluster 
generation
• The surface will ultimately 
have a very large number 
(millions to billions) of clusters
• Each cluster contains 
hundreds to thousands of 
copies of a unique fragment, 
all oriented in the same way
• We can thus proceed to 
sequence all clusters in 
parallel, achieving massive 
throughput

Illumina sequencing: Sequencing by 
synthesis
• Sequencing performed with a 
“sequencing by synthesis” 
strategy
• A primer is annealed at the 3’ of 
the tethered fragments
• Fluorescent versions of all four 
dNTPs are added at the same 
time
• These are labelled with four 
spectrally distinct fluorophores
Credit: Illumina

• The 3’ location on the dNTPs is 
protected by the fluorophores, so 
the polymerase can only add one 
of the dNTPs at a time
• Therefore, at each step, only one 
dNTP type (dATP, dTTP, dGTP, 
dCTP) will be added to each 
individual cluster
• The entire cluster will thus be 
fluorescent in the colour of that 
one dNTP
Credit: Illumina
Illumina sequencing: Sequencing by 
synthesis

• Through fluorescence imaging, we 
can thus identify which nucleotide 
has been added to each cluster
• Imaging is carried out across the 
entire surface of the flow cell, to 
capture all clusters
• We can then de-protect the added 
nucleotide by removing the 
fluorophore and repeat the process 
until we have sequenced all 
fragments (which have similar 
length)
Credit: Illumina
Illumina sequencing: Sequencing by 
synthesis

Once again: sequence 
information, for each cluster, is 
read as the sequence of “colours” 
emitted by the attached 
nucleotides
Credit: Illumina
Illumina sequencing: Sequencing by 
synthesis

• A second read can be performed by 
repeating one round of bridge PCR to 
produce again the complementary 
fragments (with the opposite orientation) 
on the surface, and removing the ones we 
already sequenced
Illumina sequencing: Sequencing by 
synthesis

Illumina sequencing: Sequence 
reconstruction
• Finally, we obtain a sequence for 
each of the fragments on the 
microarray
• If these fragments came from a 
longer construct (a gene, a plasmid, 
a chromosome…) the entire 
sequence can be reconstructed 
using bioinformatics
Illumina sequencing: Overview

• All the steps can be automated because the reaction is carried 
out in a flow cell
• Stand alone sequencers carry out all steps
Credit: Illumina
Illumina sequencing: Sequencing by 
synthesis

Illumina sequencing: Pros and cons
Pros
• High accuracy, as high as 
99.9% for sufficiently short 
fragments 
• Very high throughput: billions 
of clusters (fragments) can be 
sequenced in each run
• Low sequencing cost per 
nucleotide
Cons
• Short reads, 50-300 nt
• Workflow is time consuming. 
Library preparation, bridge PCR 
etc need to be done. 
Sequencing can take multiple 
days
• Bridge PCR can be sequence-
biased
• High cost of instrumentation 
(top-of-the range in the order of 
millions)

Third generation sequencing: Nanopores
• NGS requires amplification because 
it is hard to detect fluorescence 
from individual fragments. This 
makes sample preparation 
cumbersome
• Additionally, it is difficult with NGS to 
read long sequences, which makes 
reconstruction of gene sequences 
more challenging and prone to error
• Third generation sequencing, and 
particularly Nanopore Sequencing 
addresses these issues

Third generation sequencing: Nanopores
Principle:
• Consider a small protein pore 
inserted in a membrane, with the 
width of the channel being similar to 
the width of single-stranded DNA
• Apply an electric potential across 
the membrane, which causes an 
ionic current (ions need to be 
present)
• The ionic current can be measured 
very precisely

Third generation sequencing: Nanopores
Principle:
• Charged molecules (like DNA) will also 
be dragged through the pore
• Every time a molecule goes through the 
pore, it temporarily blocks some of the 
ions, and we can detect a dip in the 
ionic current
• The size, length and shape of the 
molecule can (with some effort) be 
inferred from the characteristics of this 
current dip (amplitude, duration etc)

Third generation sequencing: Nanopores
Principle:
• When a single-stranded DNA 
molecule goes through the pore, 
each combination of nucleotides 
passing through the pore produces a 
slightly different dip in the ionic 
current, which we can use to identify 
the bases (base calling)
• This principle can thus be used for 
sequencing

Third generation sequencing: Nanopores
Principle:
• Protein pores used have a width of the 
channel similar to that of DNA, and are 
further engineered to enhance signal-
to-noise ratio
• They are fused to a helicase enzyme, 
which serves two functions:
1.
It unwinds the double-stranded DNA, 
such that only one strand goes through 
the pore
2.
It slows down translocation to improve 
signal and facilitate base calling

Oxford nanopore technologies
• Spin-out from University of Oxford
• Portable handheld device for 
DNA/RNA sequencing
• Devices work by having an array 
of microwells, most of 
which contain a membrane with 
a single nanopore, enabling 
highly parallel sequencing
Credit: ONT

Nanopore sequencing: Pros and cons
Pros
• Ultra-long reads: can sequence 
fragments up to 100 kb
• Simple library prep and no 
amplification (no PCR). It takes 
minutes as opposed to days
• Can detect epigenetic markers
• Can sequence RNA directly
• Kit is portable and can be 
deployed for rapid diagnostics, 
even in the field (even in space)
• Kit is cheaper
Cons
• Low accuracy of the reads, in 
some cases down to 95% (vs 
99.9% for NGS)
• Systematic errors. E.g. it is 
challenging to sequence 
homopolymers (e.g. CCCCC)
• Consumables (cartridges) are 
expensive, ~$1000 each

Third generation sequencing: PacBio Single 
Molecule Real Time (SMRT) sequencing 
Principle:
• Library preparation involves adding 
hairpin adapters to circularise the 
fragments
• The instrument uses a large array of 
nano wells, each with a single DNA 
polymerase attached to it, which 
captures a single circular fragment
• Fluorescent dNTPs are included, 
which are fluorescently labelled on 
the phosphate group
Fluorophore

Third generation sequencing: PacBio Single 
Molecule Real Time (SMRT) sequencing 
Principle:
• The polymerase starts copying the 
circular DNA
• Every time the polymerase adds one 
dNTP, the fluorescent molecule is 
transiently immobilised within then 
nano well, and can be detected 
(before being released)
• Detection uses Zero Mode 
Waveguides, which enables the signal 
to be collected only from the bottom 
of the nano well, minimising noise 
from other dNTPs
Fluorophore

Third generation sequencing: PacBio Single 
Molecule Real Time (SMRT) sequencing 
Principle:
• DNA sequence can then be 
reconstructed from the sequence 
of fluorescence signal detected in 
a given nano well
• A chip of used for SMRT contains 
millions of nano wells, enabling 
high throughput
Fluorophore

Molecule Real Time (SMRT) sequencing 
• Technology developed by Pacific 
Bioscience (PacBio) in 2009

PacBio sequencing: Pros and cons
Pros
• Long reads, 10-25 kb (but not 
quite as long as nanopore)
• Highly accurate, up to 99.9%
• No amplification required
• Does well with repetitive 
sequences and 
homopolymers (contrary to 
nanopore)
Cons
• Library preparation 
(circularisation) required
• High cost per nucleotide 
compared to nanopore and 
Illumina
• Instrument expensive and 
large (not portable)
• Long experiment time (15-30 
hours)

Polymerase Chain Reaction (Review)
• Start with a (typically) double 
stranded DNA template + 
primers (forward + reverse) + 
polymerase + dNTPs + Mg2+…
• Initial denaturation (95-98 ºC, 
~1-5 min) to separate strands
• 30-40 amplification cycles
•
Denaturation (95-98 ºC, ~30 s)
•
Annealing (50-65 ºC, ~30 s), to allow 
primers to bind template
•
Extension (72 ºC, ~30 s – 2 min 
depending on length), to allow 
polymerase to extend the primers in 
the 5’ to 3’ direction
• Final extension (72 ºC, ~30 s – 2 
min depending on length), to 
ensure that all fragments are 
fully extended 
• Hold at 4 ºC
Credit: Wikipedia

Polymerase Chain Reaction (Review)
• At each cycle, the number of 
double stranded PCR 
products (defined by the two 
primers) is doubled (assuming 
an ideal process)
• At the nth cycle, we have 2𝑛 
products
• You have already learned 
about 
• Choice/design of primers
• Applications to DNA cloning (e.g. 
add target site of restriction 
enzymes)
• Applications to gene synthesis 
(PCA)
• Applications to DNA sequencing 
(library preparation)
Credit: Wikipedia

Quantitative PCR (qPCR)
• Used to detect and quantify DNA (or 
RNA)
• Like regular PCR, but we include an 
Intercalating Dye (typically SybrGreen)
• The intercalating dye will bind any 
double-stranded DNA, producing a 
fluorescent signal
• As the concentration of the amplicons 
increases over subsequent cycles, the 
fluorescent signal increases
• This is measured at every cycle (at the 
end of the extension phase)
• We thus obtain an amplification curve
• qPCR is conducted using a special PCR 
machine able to measure fluorescence 
(creatively named a qPCR machine)
Biochem (Lond) (2020) 42 (3): 48–53.

Quantitative PCR (qPCR)
• The fluorescence signal is thus 
used to detect and quantify a 
target DNA
• The amplification curve has three 
phases:
1.
Initiation phase: DNA is already 
being amplified, but the 
concentration and therefore 
fluorescent signal is too low (below 
the sensitivity of the instrument or 
the background noise)
2.
Exponential phase: The signal 
becomes large, and we can 
detect the exponential increase of 
DNA concentration (fluorescence) 
with cycle number
3.
Plateau phase: The reaction runs 
out of substrates (dNTPs) hence we 
detect saturation in signal
Biochem (Lond) (2020) 42 (3): 48–53.

Quantitative PCR (qPCR)
• The amplification curve is 
used for quantification
• A fluorescence threshold is 
defined, somewhat above 
the background noise level 
of the instrument 
• The 𝐶𝑡 (or sometimes 𝐶𝑞) 
value is the cycle number at 
which the curve intersects 
the threshold
Biochem (Lond) (2020) 42 (3): 48–53.

Small exercise
Calculate how the value of 𝐶𝑡 depends on the initial concentration (copy 
number) of the target DNA, 𝜌0

Solution
The DNA concentration vs number of cycles is given by
𝜌𝑛= 𝜌0 × 2𝑛
The fluorescent signal, 𝐹, is proportional to 𝜌𝑛
𝐹𝑛∝𝜌𝑛= 𝜌0 × 2𝑛
𝐶𝑡 is the cycle number for which 𝐹 is equal to a threshold 𝑡, hence
𝜌0 × 2𝐶𝑡∝𝑡
From which
𝐶𝑡∝log 𝑡−log 𝜌0

• The relationship 𝐶𝑡∝log 𝑡−log 𝜌0 
enables quantification
• Two methods: absolute and relative 
quantification 
• In absolute quantification we run 
qPCR for a series of samples of known 
concentration (e.g. serial dilutions, 
top), obtaining a calibration curve of 
𝐶𝑡 vs log 𝜌0 (bottom)
• For an unknown sample, we measure 
𝐶𝑡 and use the calibration curve to 
determine and absolute value of 𝜌0

• This method is also called the ΔΔ𝐶𝑡 method
• The reference DNA (gene) is required to 
account for possible experimental 
differences between the sample and 
control reactions
• The assumption is that the absolute 
amount of the target or control DNA may 
change from one experiment to the other, 
but their relative concentration with

Biochem (Lond) (2020) 42 (3): 48–53.
Quantitative PCR (qPCR)

• At the end of a qPCR reaction, the temperature 
in the sample is ramped up while measuring 
fluorescence emission
• As DNA denatures with temperature, 
fluorescence drops, producing a melting curve 
(remember Lecture 1)
• From the shape of this melting curve, we can 
learn if non-specific amplification of a non-
target construct has occurred
• If this is the case, the data will show multiple 
transitions, corresponding to the different 
melting temperatures of the different amplicons 
(likely to have different lengths)
• A simple way to determine if multiple transitions 
are present consists of computing 
Τ
−𝑑𝐹𝑑𝑇: If 
multiple melting transitions are present, one 
should see multiple peaks (or one broader 
peak, or one peak + one shoulder) 
Melting curve control

• Alternative to using intercalating dye (SybrGreen)
• It is a short DNA oligo labelled at the 5’end with a 
fluorophore and at the 3’ end with a quencher. This is 
called TaqMan probe (word pun on PacMan…)
• A quencher is a molecule that prevents the fluorophore 
from emitting light, when in the vicinity
• Because florophore and quencher are nearby on the 
probe, fluorescence emission is low
• The probe is complementary to a region on the target 
DNA, and binds to if like the primers do (but it is not 
elongated, due to the modifications)
• The Taq polymerase has nuclease activity, and while it is 
elongating one of the primers it will digest (hydrolyse) 
the TaqMan reporter it encounters
Alternative qPCR probes: TaqMan

• Degradation of the reporter induce 
fluorescence, which will thus increase 
proportionally to the concentration of the 
target DNA at every cycle
• Advantage compared to using intercalating 
dye: TaqMan is sequence specific – it will only 
bind to the target compound
• Disadvantage: more expensive (functionalised 
oligos are expensive), requires careful design 
and use of a polymerase with nuclease 
activity
Alternative qPCR probes: TaqMan

• Consists of a DNA oligo labelled with 
fluorophore and quencher at the ends, which 
forms a stem-loop (hairpin) structure
• The stem of the hairpin holds it closed, keeping 
fluorophore and quencher close to each 
other, thus suppressing fluorescence
• The loop sequence is designed to be 
complementary to the target DNA
• When target DNA is present, the beacon binds 
to it, taking fluorophore and quencher further 
apart and thus increasing fluorescence 
• Similar to the other methods, fluorescence 
increases with concentration of target DNA
Alternative qPCR probes: Molecular beacon

Alternative qPCR probes: Molecular beacon 
• Advantage compared to intercalating dye: 
selective
• Advantage compared to TaqMan: it does not 
get degraded at every cycle (it binds 
reversibly) and does not require polymerase 
with nuclease action
• Disadvantages compared to intercalating 
dye: expensive and tricky to design

Reverse Transcription (RT) qPCR
Credit: Wikipedia
• Used to detect and quantify RNA (e.g. 
mRNA or viral RNA)
• Convert RNA to complementary DNA 
(cDNA) using the enzyme reverse 
transcriptase
• For mRNA RT, we use poly T primers (12 to 18 
Ts), as these complement the 3’ poly A tail 
on mRNA
• For other RNAs (e.g. viral RNA), we use 
sequence specific primers to only reverse 
transcribe specific genes
• Once we have cDNA, we run qPCR as 
described
• RT-qPCR can be done in one step, with 
reverse transcription taking place in the 
same reaction as the qPCR

Applications: gene expression studies
• Question: determine the presence and relative 
abundance of given mRNA in a sample of 
cells or tissue
• Start by extracting and purifying all RNA
• For RT-qPCR, produce cDNA using poly-T 
primers
• Select a Reference Gene. This is something 
that cells always express at a consistent level 
to fulfil their basic function. AKA a 
housekeeping gene. 
• Run qPCR for your Gene of Interest and the 
Reference Gene, using appropriate primers

DNA and RNA aptamers
• A short DNA or RNA oligo selected to bind a specific target 
molecule
• Often used in research and, generally, biosensing, as 
simpler alternatives to antibodies
• Aptamers bind their targets with a given dissociation 
constant, 𝐾𝑑, which can vary greatly. Normally, 𝐾𝑑 is in the 
nanomolar range, but can be as low as hundreds or even 
tens of picomoles, comparable with antibodies
• The “aptamer” term was introduced by Jack Szostak (2009 
Nobel Laureate in Physiology and Medicine), coming from 
the Latin aptus, which means “to fit”
• Aptamers are selected with an in vitro process called 
Systematic Evolution of Ligands by Exponential Enrichment 
(SELEX)

The SELEX method
Biochimie 154 (2018) 132e155
• Start from a (naïve) library of ~1013-
1015 oligos. These consist of two 
constant sequences of 15-25 nt, 
which will be used a primer binding 
sites and a random sequence in 
between them
• The oligos will have random 
secondary structures
• Question: how would you 
synthesize this random library?

The SELEX method
Biochimie 154 (2018) 132e155
• Expose the library to the target, 
which can be, for instance a given 
protein
• The target is typically immobilised 
on a substrate, e.g. beads or a 
chromatography column (more on 
this later in the course)
• Oligos in the library will bind to the 
targets to different degrees, 
depending on their secondary 
structures and therefore sequence

The SELEX method
Biochimie 154 (2018) 132e155
• We wash to remove unbound 
sequence
• We then elute, changing solvent 
conditions (e.g. changing ionic 
strength, pH or temperature) such 
that we force the detachment of 
the strongly bound oligos, which 
we recover
• The recovered oligo pool is now 
enriched in the strongly binding 
oligos

The SELEX method
Biochimie 154 (2018) 132e155
• We perform PCR or RT-PCR (for RNA 
aptamers) to amplify the recovered oligo 
pool
• For RNA aptamers, we use in vitro 
transcription (more on this later in the 
course) to produce RNA from the cDNA 
obtained with RT-qPCR
• Repeat the whole SELEX cycle 10-15 times
• At every cycle, we further (exponentially) 
enrich the library in the strong binders
• After the final cycle, we sequence the 
pool to identify aptamers that have 
emerged
• We would typically characterise their 
binding to the target to measure the 𝐾𝑑

The Cell SELEX method
Biochimie 154 (2018) 132e155
• Variation of the SELEX method, in 
which we select against whole cells as 
targets
• Useful for, e.g., drug delivery 
applications
• It is not known to what, on the cell 
surface, the oligos are binding
• Would typically include negative 
selection steps, to eliminate from the 
library oligos that bind to cells other 
than the target cells
• This is useful, for instance, to select 
aptamers that bind only to a given cell 
type (e.g. cancer cell), and do not 
recognise other cells (e.g.  non-
cancerous)

Applications: therapeutics
• FDA approve drug Pegaptanib 
(Macugen)
• Chemically modified RNA aptamer 
used in the treatment of macular 
degeneration, an eye condition 
• Binds to a factor (VEGF) contributing 
to angiogenesis (making new blood 
vessels), one of the processes behind 
the disease
• Pegaptanib is injected in the eye, 
where it binds to VEGF acting as 
antagonist
Nature Reviews Drug Discovery 5, 123–132 (2006)

applications to cancer therapeutics
• For these applications, aptamers are

be degraded by nucleases
• Therefore, the oligos are often 
chemically modified (e.g. 
methylated, pegylated) to limit 
degradation

DNA nanotechnology
•
DNA nanotechnology is a collection of tools and methods 
(experimental, theoretical, computational) that exploits the 
physical and chemical properties of DNA (and RNA) to 
control structure and dynamics at the nanoscale 
•
Applications to healthcare, sensing, materials, microscopy, 
synthetic biology...
•
Traditionally, it is divided in structural and dynamic DNA 
nanotechnology

“Not merely the secret of life”
We learned (extensively) about the 
biological role of DNA, but DNA has 
many interesting properties as a material
• Chemically stable and not easily 
degraded (different from RNA)
• DNA oligos with arbitrary sequence can 
be chemically synthesised, at 
decreasing price
• Synthetic DNA can be easily chemically 
modified (e.g. to append fluorophores, 
quenchers, linkers for conjugation)

“Not merely the secret of life”
• Interesting polymer physics 
properties (single stranded DNA is 
much more flexible than double-
stranded DNA)
• Nucleic acid thermodynamics is very 
well understood and predictable 
(recall simple models for computing 
Δ𝐺0, 𝑇𝑚…)
• DNA hybridisation is thermally 
reversible under near-environmental 
conditions

Base pairing selectivity
• Base pairing interactions are exquisitely selective
• Consider two complementary 12 nt strands at equal concentration of 
1 μM and 𝑇= 293.15 K. Hybridisation free energy and melting 
temperature are (for the specific sequence I chose): ∆𝐺= −16.8 kcal 
mol−1, 𝑇𝑚= 53.2℃
• Now consider two random 12 nt strands in the same conditions. For 
these, I calculated: ∆𝐺= −2.9 kcal mol−1, 𝑇𝑚= −30.7℃
• Note the massive difference in hybridisation free energy and melting 
temperature. Complementary strands need to me heated up to over 
50℃ for melting, non-complementary strands would not hybridise unless 
you cool them way below room temperature

Sequence orthogonality
•
For a DNA 𝑁-mer the number of possible sequences is 4𝑁 
•
For a 12-mer, this is 1.7 × 107 different sequences
•
Of these most will barely interact with each other (high ∆𝐺, low 
𝑇𝑚), while only a small sub-set would be somewhat 
complementary
•
Possibility of designing a very large number of molecules with 
orthogonal interactions!

•

•
Unbinding rates of oligos depend on

•
This is undesirable! It would be much

Toehold-mediated strand displacement
•
The objective is breaking the duplex S 
and forming a new duplex L, in which 
strand X (invader) has replaced strand Y 
(incumbent)
•
Thermal dissociation of duplex S would 
take a very long time because of the 
high free energy cost of unbinding 
several bases.
•
Toehold-mediated strand displacement 
(TMSD) catalyzes the process of switching 
bonds by co-localizing X and S using a 
toehold (domains h and its 
complementary h*)
Simmel et al. Chem. Rev 119, 6326−6369, 2019

Toehold-mediated strand displacement
Simmel et al. Chem. Rev 119, 6326−6369, 2019 
A) S and X are in solution
B) Domain h in X binds to h* in S
C) X starts to displace Y one base at the time
D) The displacement proceeds through a 
three-way branch migration process. This 
is a diffusive process rather than thermally 
activated, and can go either way
E) Eventually, branch migration proceeds in 
the desired direction and is completed
F) Y is released and duplex L is formed

Toehold-mediated strand displacement
Simmel et al. Chem. Rev 119, 6326−6369, 2019 
•
The final step (E-F) is irreversible, because 
there is no toehold for the reverse reaction
•
If h and h* are sufficiently long, TMSD can 
be much faster than duplex exchange 
mediated by thermal denaturation. This is 
because the free energy barrier for the 
process is much lower! : at no point 
domains b and b* detach completely
•
TMSD is thermodynamically driven. Duplex 
S has fewer base-pairs than duplex L
•
However, the rate of the displacement is 
(more or less) independent on the absolute 
stability of the duplexes, as determined by 
domains b and b*!

Protein folding
• Tertiary structure is defined by the amino acid 
sequence – no help required
• Levinthal – 100 residues, sample 3 
Ramachandran angles = 3198 conformations
• Proteins fold in milliseconds!
• Native conformation is the most stable, but 
energy difference between folded and denatured 
small (20-40 kJ/mol)
• Hydrophobic effect critical but also hydrogen 
bonding, electrostatic etc.
• Folding follows limited number of pathways – 
‘folding funnel’ energy landscape
• Intermediate state – molten globules (but not 
always)

Structure solution from diffracted X-rays 
• Objective is to determine the arrangement 
of protein atoms in space
• Electron density in the unit cell (of the 
crystal) is related to the Fourier transform 
of the amplitude and phase of the scatted 
X-rays
• Reverse process - Fourier synthesis – can 
be used to reconstruct an  electron density 
map of the unit cell
• Amplitude is square root of intensities of 
diffraction spots
• Phase information is lost – ‘the phase 
problem’

Structure solution from diffracted X-rays 
• Max Perutz solved the phase problem by 
incorporating a few heavy atoms into 
haemoglobin crystals
• Result – a shift in the intensity of all 
diffraction spots
• Multiple Isomorphous Replacement 
permits retrieval of phase information
• John Kendrew – Perutz’ PhD student – used 
the technique to solve the first protein 
structure (myoglobin, at 6 Å)
• Later extended to 2 Å - required 
computation for calculations

AlphaFold: High-level overview

Inputs
Jumper, J et al. Highly accurate protein structure prediction with AlphaFold. Nature (2021).

The role of multiple sequence alignment (MSA)
•
The primary input for AlphaFold2’s neural network is then the MSA.
•
AlphaFold2 uses MSAs to compare and analyse the sequences of similar proteins from different 
organisms. It highlights similarities and differences, which helps understand the evolutionary 
relationships between the proteins.

Co-evolution
If two amino acids in a protein are in close contact, mutations in one of them will probably be 
followed by mutations of the other. This preserves the structure of the protein, and is known as co-
evolution or covariation.
The opposite is also true: if two regions of a protein are changing and evolving independently from 
each other, it is likely that they are not in direct contact.

Evoformer
Jumper, J et al. Highly accurate protein structure prediction with AlphaFold. Nature (2021).
The Evoformer interprets and updates both the MSA and the pair representations. The important aspect of this network is 
the continuous flow of information between the MSA and the pair representations. This enables reasoning about spatial and 
evolutionary relationships, which refines the structural hypothesis.

Structure module
Jumper, J et al. Highly accurate protein structure prediction with AlphaFold. Nature (2021).

Recycling
Jumper, J et al. Highly accurate protein structure prediction with AlphaFold. Nature (2021).

AlphaFold structures closely resemble crystal structures
•

the predicted structures, like protein domains) work well as search models for molecular 
replacement (MR) in X-ray crystallography.
•
Molecular replacement works well if RMSD < 1-1.5 Å for at least 30% of the atoms.
•
Availability of high-accuracy models is then definitely critical for successful structure

What is bioprocessing?
• Bioprocessing is the use of biological catalysts in the form of live 
cells (bacteria, plants, fungi, animal cells) or their constituents 
(enzymes), for the production or transformation of a product
• It is an essential component to many food, chemical and 
pharma industries, and has been for a long time…

Developing a microorganism for 
bioprocessing
• Example is for a recombinant product (protein) 
that can be encoded in DNA
• Gene of interest is identified in a cell, and 
extracted
• Gene is cloned into a plasmid
• Cells (in the example E. coli) are transformed 
with the plasmid, so they produce the target 
recombinant protein
• Cell used is chosen for its ability to produce 
efficiently the target product, but also based on 
how easy it is to culture at scale, harvest etc. 
Engineering considerations made at this stage
• You have learned all about this!

Scaling up
• Microorganism development is done primarily in 
very small cultures of a few hundreds of microliters 
(well-plates), followed by small-scale cultures in 
flasks (250 ml to 1l)
• At this stage, medium composition, pH, 
temperature, and other environmental conditions 
allowing optimal growth and productivity are 
determined
• The performance of the organism is determined 
using parameters such as growth rate, and product 
yield

Scaling up
• Once growth parameters are known, scaling up 
starts with a bench-top bioreactor (1-2l)
• In the bioreactor we can control and measure 
parameters such as stirrer speed, dissolved oxygen 
concentration, pH and temperature.
• Better control compared to flasks, allows better 
characterization of optimal growth conditions and 
collecting information on shear sensitivity, oxygen 
requirements, foaming etc.
• Important process parameters can be measured or 
computed, including oxygen transfer rate, power 
number, Reynolds number, mixing time etc.

Scaling up
• We then move to a pilot-scale bioreactor (100-
1000l)
• Usually this is geometrically similar to the bench-
top reactor. Rates of air sparging and stirring 
may change to enable sufficient oxygen 
transfer and fit power requirements
• Changes, often loss, of productivity may occur 
and need to be assessed at this stage

Upstream processing
• If pilot-scale testing is successful, one proceeds 
to designing and industrial scale plant, where 
many considerations around auxiliary facilities 
need to be made (air supply, sterilization, 
cooling water supply, medium preparation),
• Preparation and sterilization of media
• Fermentation or cell-free bioprocesses 
conducted in the designed bioreactors
• Bioreactors designed considering requirements 
for (gentle) mixing, oxygenation, temperature, 
foam reduction, energy efficiency. 
• You have learned about this in the reactors 
courses

Downstream processing
• 10 – 300 m3 of fermentation broth
• Mainly water – the fraction of product 
could be high, but also as low as parts 
per billion
• Incredibly complex mixtures of cells, 
proteins, sugars and other 
macromolecules, many of which are 
chemically similar to the desired 
product
• We need to extract and purify the 
product!

Downstream processing
The treatment of culture broth after completion of 
fermentation is known as downstream processing
• Downstream processing is typically concerned with 
separation and concentration of the desired product 
• Typically, no further chemical transformations occur
• Separations in a biological context can be challenging for 
a variety of reasons (next slide)
• Can account for the major proportion of the total 
production cost

• Fermentation products are often formed in dilute solution 
– both cell culture media and cells comprise mainly of 
water
• Biological products are labile – this restricts the suitable 
range of temperatures, pressures, solvents and salt 
concentrations for product recovery 
• Bio products are susceptible to contamination – it is 
usually not feasible to maintain aseptic conditions 
throughout the entire process plant
• Downstream processing must be quick and efficient to 
avoid product degradation
Challenges with downstream processing

Separation techniques in bioprocessing can be classified into the following five stages:
1. Cell removal: this is commonly the first step after fermentation. Products could be 
within the cell, outside the cell, or the cells may be the product. In any case, 
separating the cells from the fermentation media is a major step in product 
recovery. Typical unit operations comprise filtration or centrifugation. Covered in 
this course.
2. Cell disruption: when the products are intra-cellular, cells must be lysed. This can 
be achieved using mechanical, physical (non-mechanical), chemical or 
enzymatic methods. The remaining cell debris must then be removed using the 
aforementioned cell removal methods. Covered in this course.
Downstream processing separation stages

3. Primary isolation: the aim of the primary isolation stage is to remove 
components with substantially different properties to the product of 
interest. Primary isolation processes are usually non-selective and depend 
on the chemical and physical properties of the product. Typical operations 
include solvent extraction, two-phase liquid extraction, adsorption, 
precipitation (covered in this course) or ultrafiltration (done in separations)
4. Product enrichment: these are highly selective methods that separate 
products from impurities with similar physical or chemical properties. 
Different types of chromatography are commonly used for product 
enrichment (covered in this course).
5. Final isolation: the final form of the product will vary depending on the 
application. Generally, liquid products are processed via ultrafiltration and 
solid products crystallised before centrifugation or filtration and drying 
(done in this separations).
Downstream processing separation stages

Downstream processing separation stages
At each step, product concentration and purity 
increase steeply

Downstream process logic
Process to be tailored to specific needs, but process logic can be 
generalised as shown in below

• Downstream processing can account for a substantial 
proportion of the total production cost of a fermentation 
product 
• The ratio of fermentation cost to product recovery cost for 
well characterised antibiotics such as penicillin is 60:40, 
however, for many bio products, such as recombinant 
proteins or monoclonal antibodies, this ratio is reversed 
and can be up to 20:80
Cost of downstream processing

Cost of downstream processing
• For certain compounds 
initial concentration is very 
low, which increases 
recovery costs and thus 
selling price
• This leaves an open ground 
for innovation
• Chemical engineers have 
the potential to level the 
cost scale in many modern 
biological processes

Cell removal
• Cell removal unit operations essentially separate particulates 
from the fermentation broth or other liquids 
• Filtration and centrifugation procedures achieve this by 
exploiting particle size and density, respectively 
• In some cases, the fermentation broth is pre-treated to 
improve the efficiency of separation, e.g. by including 
additives that reduce viscosity and/or promote cell 
aggregation
• In this lecture we introduce filtration, covering the basics of 
design and operation as applied to bioprocessing.
• Centrifugation will be examined in Lecture 10
Downstream process logic

Dead-end filtration
• 'Dead-end’ filtration is perhaps the 
simplest form of solid-liquid separation 
• Simple principle; a physical barrier with 
openings smaller than the suspended 
particles impedes motion of the latter, 
whereas the liquid can flow past the 
particles resulting in the separation of 
the two phases 
• This process can be promoted by 
gravity or by pressure drop

Pre-coating filters and filter aids
• Filter is usually a “filter cloth”
• A filter cake is progressively formed on the cloth. 
The cake aids filter efficiency, but also increases 
flow resistance
• Filter aids, e.g. Kieselguhr particles can be 
added to the broth. These are naturally 
occurring materials used to make the cake more 
porous and decrease resistance
• The cloth can be pre-coated with filter aid 
particles

• The major problem with dead-end filtration is cake 
formation during the process 
• As the cake forms, it deteriorates the performance of the 
filter by imposing a greater resistance to liquid flow 
• Eventually, the liquid flow will drop to zero if the pressure 
difference is not increased 
• To overcome this issue, filter aids are used, e.g. Kieselguhr 
particles can be added to the broth or used to precoat 
the filter in order to increase cake porosity, as mentioned 
earlier
Issues with dead-end filtration

Batch filtration: plate and frame filter 
press
• Cloth spread out over plates, which 
support the cloth along ridges leaving at 
the same time a free area below the cloth 
for flow of the filtrate.
• Larger number of plates gives sufficient 
area
• Cake builds up on the upstream side of 
the cloth
• When available space between plates if 
filled with cake, the filter press needs to be 
dismantled and scraped off

• Conventional plate filters are also laborious to operate, as the 
filter must be frequently serviced for the removal of the filter 
cake 
• This makes them suitable for small batch fermentation 
processes
• For large fermentation processes, continuous rotary drum 
vacuum filters are more commonly used
Issues with batch dead-end filtration

Continuous rotary drum vacuum filter
• Commonly applied for dead-end filtration
• Can process large volumes
• Ideal for separation of organisms
• Difficult to operate aseptically

• Horizontal cylindrical drum of 0.5  to 3 m 
in diameter is covered with filter cloth 
and rotated slowly at 0.1 to 2 rpm 
• A vacuum is applied inside the drum, 
drawing liquid from the immersed 
portion to the interior of the drum 
• As the drum rotates out of the reservoir, 
the filter cake is sprayed with wash liquid 
• Continued application of vacuum results 
in the cake being dewatered before 
removal with a scraper
• The liquid is drawn through the cloth and 
collected in a separate tank 
Cheap and easy but not aseptic

Downstream process logic

Centrifugation
• Like filtration, separates solids from liquid medium
• Works by rotating the sample so to produce high 
centrifugal acceleration, which causes particles to 
sediment out of the liquid phase
• Most effective
oLarge particles
oLow liquid viscosity 
oLarge density difference between the particles and 
liquid

Centrifugation
• Conditions may not be easy to establish with cell cultures (cells may 
not be very dense, media can be dense, bacterial cells are small)
• Limitations are overcome by designing large centrifuges that 
operate at high rotational speeds, although physical and safety 
limitations can limit size and operation

Types of centrifuge
• Centrifuges can be classified on the design of their 
internal structure/geometry
• We will discuss two types:
1. Tubular bowl centrifuge
2. Disc stack bowl centrifuge

Tubular bowl centrifuge
• Commonly used in food and bio-pharma
• The equipment consists of a rotating tube 
and a nozzle at the base of the unit where 
feed is introduced 
• As particles flow upwards, they are spun 
outwards, colliding with the walls of the 
bowl
• The liquid continues to flow upwards, 
leaving via a weir at the top of the bowl

Tubular bowl centrifuge
• The time that it takes from the liquid to exit 
the top of the tube is the residence time, 
which decreases with increasing flow rate
• Over a sedimentation time, centrifugal 
force will cause the particles to migrate 
towards the wall of the tube
• The sedimentation time is faster for greater 
rotations speed (larger/denser particles, 
lower viscosity…)
• Particles are efficiently separated if the 
sedimentation time is shorter than the 
residence time

• Batch centrifugation is common for 
tubular bowl centrifuge: the solids need 
to be removed once they fill the tube 
up to the escape point of the liquid
• Some models an operate as continuous 
process (scheme on the right), using a 
heavy-phase outlet close to the outer 
wall
Tubular bowl centrifuge

• Useful for difficult separations that require 
high centrifugal forces – up to 16000 g
• Foaming can be a problem
• Easy to clean
Tubular bowl centrifuge

• Centrifuge contain conical shear sheets of metal 
that are stacked on top of each other with 
clearances of approximately 0.3 mm
• As the bowl rotates, the discs split liquid into layers 
• The denser liquid containing the solids is displaced 
outwards whereas lighter liquid remains close to 
the centre 
• Both streams are withdrawn from the centrifuge as 
shown in the figure on the left 
• Solids can be removed periodically from nozzles 
(batch mode) or continuously from the heavy-
liquid discharge outlet (continuous mode, more 
common)
Disc-stack centrifuge

• Foam can be controlled 
• Difficult to clean compared to tube 
bowl
• Easier to use in continuous mode 
compared with tubular bowl
Disc-stack centrifuge
Disc-stack Vs tubular

Centrifugation vs filtration
Centrifugation
Pros: 
• Easier to make sterile
• No consumables cost
• Easier to run in continuous mode
Cons:
• Higher capital cost
• Many moving parts/seals that can 
fail
• Safety
Filtration
Pros: 
• Lower capital costs
• Easier to separate small cells
Cons:
• Nonsterile
• Consumables costs (filters)

Cell-disruption strategies
There are many approaches to cell disruption 
• Mechanical methods (this lecture)
• Bead mill
• Ultrasonication
• French press
• High pressure homogenizer
• Non-mechanical physical methods (next lecture)
• Thermolysis

Cell-disruption strategies
• Some methods are only applicable at small- or lab-scale, 
others scalable
• Different methods may be better suited for different types of 
cells
• Different cells are intrinsically easier or more challenging to 
disrupt
• E.g. bacteria and yeast (in particular) have tough cell walls 
difficult to disrupt. Bacteria are small, meaning that they are 
more difficult to disrupt with mechanical means only
• Mammalian cell lines only have a plasma membrane and no 
cell wall, so they are easily disrupted

Cell walls
• Microorganisms used in bioprocessing are often surrounded by tough cell 
walls 
• Gram + bacteria (e.g. L. lactis) have a thick peptidoglycan wall. Gram – 
bacteria (e.g. E. coli) have a thinner peptidoglycan wall, but it is 
enveloped by an outer membrane rich in lipopolysaccharides (LPS)

Cell walls
Saccharomyces cervisiae cell wall. World's Poultry Science Journal,  73,  2017
• Yeast (e.g. S. cervisiae) has a thick wall with multiple layers, 
including polysaccharides, and chitin. It makes yeast very difficult to 
disrupt

• Can be used at lab and industrial 
scale
• Semi-continuous process

Cell-disruption strategies

• Bead mill

Non-mechanical physical methods
• Include thermal, decompression and osmotic shock
• Costly and difficult to scale up, therefore used mostly at 
lab rather than production scale

Non-mechanical physical methods: 
Thermolysis
• Cells can be disrupted by heating. E.g. cytoplasmic 
proteins can be extracted form E. coli if kept at 90°C for 10 
minutes
• Cells can be disrupted by freeze-thaw cycles, due to 
formation of ice crystals that disrupt cell membranes/walls
• Both these techniques are energy intensive and therefore 
not very suitable for production scale processes

Non-mechanical physical methods: 
Decompression
• Cells are exposed to high-
pressure gas that solubilizes in 
the medium and distributes itself 
also within the cells
• Upon rapid decompression, the 
gas within the cells expands, 
causing disruption
Decompression chamber (Anton-Parr)

Non-mechanical physical methods: 
Osmotic shock
 
• Cells exposed to hypertonic or hypotonic 
conditions.
• Hypertonic conditions are typically 
obtained by adding salts (~1M 
concentration) and cause the cells to shrink 
rapidly as water leaves the cytoplasm. The 
process may disrupt the cells
• Hypotonic conditions are obtained by 
diluting in pure water, causing water to flow 
into the cytoplasm.  Cells can burst in the 
process
• Not sufficiently efficient for production-
scale. Added salt also needs to be 
removed, which adds to cost

Non-physical (chemical and 
biological) methods
• Non-physical methods disrupt cell walls and membranes 
through the addition of chemical substances (solvents, 
detergents) or biological agents(enzymes)
• Multiple substances can be combined to achieve the 
desired efficiency
• Drawbacks compared to physical methods is the cost of 
the substances used, and that these may need to be 
removed

Chemical methods: Detergents
 
• Detergents, or surfactants, can 
solubilize the phospholipid cell 
membranes through micellization and 
by solubilizing membrane proteins
• Typical detergents used are sodium 
dodecyl sulfate (SDS) and Triton X100
• Detergents may need to be removed 
for later processing stages, adding to 
cost
• Commonly used at lab-scale for RNA 
or DNA extraction

Chemical methods: Solvents
• Solvents such as alcohols, dimethyl sulfoxide, methyl ethyl ketone 
or toluene can solubilize the lipid components in the cell 
membrane, causing their disruption
• Like detergents, also solvents may need to be removed for later 
processing stages
• Solvents may cause denaturation of target proteins, which may 
be undesirable
• Use of solvents may be combined with alkaline compounds used 
to hydrolyze the cell wall

Biological methods: Enzymes
• Utilizes enzymes to digest cell walls
• Enzymes include lysozyme, cellulase, protease, chitinase, 
pectinase (and more)
• It is specific: different enzymes can be used to digest different 
parts of the cell wall. For instance lysozyme is used to hydrolyze 
the peptidoglycan layer in bacteria, chitinase for yeast cell wall 
and pectinase for plant cell wall
• Can be combined with detergents. E.g. for gram – bacteria 
lysozyme treatment follows detergent treatment used to 
remove the outer membrane and expose the peptidoglycan 
layer
• Enzymes are costly, limiting application in production-scale 
processes

Cell-debris removal (centrifugation, 
filtration)

Downstream process logic

Primary Isolation
• We are left with feed that is either a liquor from which the micro-
organisms have been removed OR a cell homogenate
• The target products of interest (e.g.  proteins, peptides, small molecules 
such as antibiotics…) are in solution along with many non-desirable 
components
• The aim of primary isolation stage is to remove components with 
substantially different properties to the product of interest
• Primary isolation processes are usually not very selective and depend 
on the chemical and physical properties of the product

Primary Isolation methods

In this lecture and part of the next we are going to give an overview 
of the principles and applicability of these methods

I. Solvent extraction
• The aqueous feed contains a target 
organic compound A
• It is mixed with an organic solvent, 
immiscible with the aqueous feed,  
within which A preferentially 
partitions
• The system is agitated to allow 
transfer of A to the solvent and left 
to settle
• Solvent and aqueous phase are 
separated
• A is recovered from the solvent, e.g. 
through evaporation

I. Solvent extraction
• Solvent is chosen so that A partitions 
strongly within it, but undesirable 
compounds in the feed (e.g. cell 
debris) do not.
• Often used for extracting 
biopharmaceuticals
• E.g. penicillin can be extracted from 
aqueous broths using solvents such 
as butyl or amyl acetate.

I. Solvent extraction
• In a plant-scale process, solvent 
extraction is often carried out in 
continuous mode rather than batch 
mode
• A countercurrent centrifuge can be 
used for this. The heavy phase (typically 
the feed) is mixed with the light phase 
(typically solvent) by agitators at the 
bottom, enabling transfer of the target 
compound from one phase to the 
other. A centrifuge then separates and 
recovers the two phases

II. Aqueous two-phase extraction
• Similar principle to solvent extraction, 
but here we exploit liquid-liquid phase 
separation between two aqueous 
phases rather than organic solvents
• Phase separation can be induced by 
adding solutes such as polymers of 
different chemistry, and salts
• Solutions contacting poly-ethylene 
glycol (PEG) and salts will separate in 
salt-rich and PEG rich phases (top)
• Solutions of PEG+Dextran will separate in 
PEG-rich and Dextran-rich phases 
(bottom)
Azevedo et al, Trends in Biotechnology 27, 4 2009

• Often used in pharma, e.g. for 
separation of monoclonal 
antibodies, growth factors and 
hormones
• Target compounds will partition in 
one or the other phases depending 
on their physical and chemical 
characteristics
• Degree of partitioning can be fine 
tuned by changing system 
composition (adding salts, changing 
polymer MW)
• Easily scalable
Azevedo et al, Trends in Biotechnology 27, 4 2009

III. Precipitation
• We induce aggregation of the target 
compound, which then precipitates 
and can be easily extracted using e.g. 
further filtration or centrifugation.
• Often used for proteins
• Precipitation can remove large 
amounts of water
• However, only partial purification is 
achieved since molecules of similar 
characteristics will precipitate together
Wikimedia commons

III. Precipitation
• Precipitation is induced by a 
decrease in the solubility of the 
compound upon addition of 
salts, solvents or polymers, or in 
response to changes in pH
• These additives or changes in 
surface chemistry of the 
compounds make interactions 
with water less favorable causing 
aggregation
Wikimedia commons

III. Precipitation
In bioprocessing, there are four main 
methods used to achieve 
precipitation, primarily to recover 
proteins. These are:
a) Salting out
b) Isoelectric precipitation
c) Polymer precipitation
d) Organic solvent precipitation
Let’s discuss them one by one
Wikimedia commons

• Solubility of molecules with hydrophobic regions 
(e.g. proteins) depends on salt concentration.
• Solubility is low at low salt concentration, peaks at 
intermediate concentration, and then drops again 
at very high concentration. 
• The process of resuspending molecules by adding 
salt is referred to as salting-in, while that causing 
precipitation is called salting-out, and is relevant 
for protein precipitation in bioprocessing
• Different proteins will salt out at different salt 
concentrations depending on their 
hydrophobicity. 
III. Precipitation: a) Salting out
Wikimedia commons

• Salting out happens because ions, and 
particularly anions, interfere with solvation 
by water
• Water molecules form a solvation shell 
around proteins, which prevents 
aggregation
• At higher salt concentration, anions will bind 
more often to water, making it less available 
to form the solvation shell and thus 
prompting aggregation
• Solvation is also important for the secondary 
and tertiary structure of proteins. High salt 
may also cause protein unfolding
III. Precipitation: a) salting out
Org. Process Res. Dev. 2017, 21, 1355−1370

• Different anions have different 
effectiveness for inducing salting out. 
• They are normally ranked as:
F−≈SO4
−> HPO4
−> C2H3O2
−> Cl−>
Br−> NO3
−> ClO3
−> I−> ClO4
−> SCN−
• This was discovered by Franz 
Hofmeister, and it is known as the 
Hofmeister series.
• The origin of these differences is still 
matter of research!

and salt used, and 𝐶𝑆 is the salt concentration. 𝛽𝑆 is also a

III. Precipitation: b) isoelectric
• Proteins most often carry net electric charge or are 
zwitterionic (net charge is zero, but parts of the protein are 
positively or negatively charged)
• Charge is important to stabilize proteins against aggregation, 
due to Coulomb repulsion that counteracts hydrophobic 
interactions
• Charge is pH dependent due to (de)protonation of charged 
amino acids. At low pH it is more likely that a protein be 
positively charged. At high pH it is more likely negatively 
charged

• The Isoelectric point, pI, is the pH at 
which a given protein is neutral
• Different amino acids have 
different pI (right)
• The pI of a protein depends on its 
composition, but it is usually 
between 4 and 6
III. Precipitation: b) isoelectric

• Solubility of proteins as a function of pH 
therefore has a minimum as shown on the 
right
• Isoelectric precipitation works by 
changing (typically reducing) the pH of 
the feed until the protein of interest 
reaches minimum solubility and 
precipitates
• Advantage over salting out: de-salting 
step is not required 
• Drawback: similar to salting out, reaching 
the isoelectric point may lead to protein 
denaturation
Solubility of soybean vicilin (7S) protein as 
a function of pH. The protein isoelectric 
point is close to pH 5.0. 
J. Agric. Food Chem. 50, 49534958. 
III. Precipitation: b) isoelectric

Example of isoelectric precipitation: 
removing proteins in sugar processing 
• Washing, grinding and filtering sugar 
beets leaves a feed rich in sugar and 
various proteins
• We wish to precipitate the proteins and 
keep the sugar
• A gradient of pH is established in a 
horizontal tank with stirrers
• In each compartment a different 
protein pI equal to the pH at that 
point precipitates
• A protein-free sugar solution is finally 
produced
• Process used at British Sugar plant in 
Bury St Edmunds

III. Precipitation: c) polymer-induced
• Neutral polymers such as PEG and Dextran can lead to 
protein precipitation following a principle similar to salting 
out: polymers at high concentration attract water 
molecules away from the solvation shell of proteins (they 
act like ”solvent sponges”) leading to aggregation
• Not to be confused with aqueous two-phase extraction

• In addition, PEG can also lead to protein aggregation of large globular 
proteins by inducing depletion forces first explained by Asakura and Oosawa
• This entropic effect arises because small particles (PEG) are excluded from 
the volume between two adjacent large particles (proteins)
• There is therefore a larger osmotic pressure from the polymer outside this gap 
than inside, leading to attractive forces between the proteins
PEG 
Protein 
III. Precipitation: c) polymer-induced
Asakura and Oosawa, On Interaction between Two Bodies Immersed in a Solution of Macromolecules, 
J. Chem. Phys. 22, 1255 (1954)

• The feed is mixed with a miscible solvent, e.g. ethanol or methanol 
• Different from solvent extraction, where we used immiscible solvents
• In sufficiently high molar fraction, the solvent displaces the water 
molecules from the solvation shell around the proteins, disrupting it and 
casing the proteins to aggregate, similar to what happens with salting 
out and polymer-induced precipitation
• To be more precise, ethanol or methanol will decrease the dielectric 
constant of water (but this is beyond the scope of the course)
• Often used for primary isolation of antibodies

IV. Adsorption
• Adsorption is a surface process where components 
of a gas or liquid bind to solid surfaces via physical or 
chemical interactions (van der Walls, electrostatic)
• The compound that binds is called adsorbate, while 
the material to which the adsorbate binds is called 
adsorbant
• Adsorption is often used as primary isolation method, 
particularly in pharma for the separation of proteins, 
amino-acids, antibodies and enzymes. It is also used 
in the treatment of waste-waters
• The adsorbant is normally porous particles with very 
high surface area for adsorption, packed in a 
column. Materials include activated charcoal and 
resins made from styrene, divinylbenzene, or 
acrylamide polymers

IV. Adsorption
• There are four main stages in isolation by 
adsorption 
1. Binding: the sample is contacted with the 
adsorbant, and the adsorbate binds
2. Washing: the adsorbant is washed to remove 
unbound and weakly bound compounds
3. Elution: the adsobate is made to unbind so it 
can be recovered. This is normally done by 
flowing a different solvent that reverses the 
interactions that lead to adsorption in the first 
place
4. Regeneration: the adsorbant is brought back 
to its original conditions so it can be re-used, 
for instance by replacing the elution solvent 
with the original binding solvent

Binding phase
• An adsorption zone 
propagates downwards, at 
a rate slower than the liquid 
flow. In this zone, adsorption 
is occurring, and the resin is 
not yet saturated
• Above this zone, the resin is 
saturated
• Feed comes out from the 
other side of the column 
(effluent) with a time-
dependent 𝐶𝐴
From P.M. Doran, “Bioprocess Engineering Principles” 
Academic Press, 2nd ed. 2012.

• At early times, when the 
adsorption zone has not yet 
reached the bottom of the 
colum, 𝐶𝐴 is low
• At late times, the adsorption 
and saturation zones reach the 
bottom of the column. The 
column becomes saturated and 
𝐶𝐴 starts increasing
• The point when the 𝐶𝐴 starts 
increasing is the “breakpoint”
• The process is usually terminated 
at this stage, to avoid wasting 
target compound in the effluent
From P.M. Doran, “Bioprocess Engineering Principles” 
Academic Press, 2nd ed. 2012.
